card.title: Foundations of good code checkpoint
card.blurb: The Part five checkpoint: good names, no duplication, one job per function, readability and comments. Pass it to close the foundations of good code.
hero.title: Foundations of good code checkpoint
intro.0: The checkpoint for Part five. Answer a handful of questions on the habits of good code - names, duplication, one job per function, writing for the reader, and comments - to lock them in and earn your XP.
quiz.title: Part five checkpoint
quiz.metaLabel: Foundations of good code · Part five checkpoint
quiz.intro: Six questions drawn from Part five - the habits of good code. Pick the best answer for each, then submit. Score four or more to pass and earn XP; a fresh set is drawn each time you retry.
question.1.stem: What makes a name like timeoutSeconds better than t?
question.1.option.0: It says what the value holds, so the code explains itself
question.1.option.1: It makes the program run faster
question.1.why: A good name says what a value holds or what a function does, so a reader does not have to guess.
question.2.stem: A function named check() is awkward to work with mainly because...
question.2.option.0: Its name does not say what it checks, so you must open it to find out
question.2.option.1: The CPU cannot run functions with short names
question.2.option.3: A function may not be named with one word
question.2.why: A name should say what a function does; check() forces the reader to open it to learn its job.
question.3.stem: Why is copy-pasting the same logic into two places risky?
question.3.option.0: A later fix must be made in every copy, and one is easy to miss
question.3.option.2: The compiler refuses to build duplicated code
question.3.option.3: It uses twice as much memory while running
question.3.why: Duplication spreads one piece of knowledge across many places, so a change has to be repeated and a copy can be forgotten.
question.4.stem: "Don't repeat yourself" suggests that a rule used in several places should be...
question.4.option.0: Put in one named function that each place calls
question.4.option.1: Copied carefully so every copy matches
question.4.option.2: Deleted from all but one place
question.4.option.3: Marked with a comment above each copy
question.4.why: DRY keeps each piece of knowledge in a single place, so you fix it once and every caller gets the fix.
question.5.stem: What is the benefit of a function that does just one job?
question.5.option.0: It earns a clear name and can be reused on its own
question.5.option.1: It always has fewer lines than any other function
question.5.option.2: It never needs to be checked
question.5.option.3: It runs on more operating systems
question.5.why: A single-purpose function is easy to name, reuse and check in isolation - the everyday seed of the single-responsibility idea.
question.6.stem: Why prefer a plain multi-line version over a clever one-liner that does the same thing?
question.6.option.0: Code is read far more than written, so clarity saves every reader time
question.6.why: Readability is how quickly a reader understands code; since code is read more than written, clear usually beats clever.
question.7.option.0: One that explains why - a reason the code cannot show
question.7.option.1: One that repeats what the line already says
question.7.option.2: One that just restates the variable name
question.7.option.3: A comment is never worth keeping
question.7.why: Good comments capture the reason (why); a comment that repeats the code adds nothing and goes stale.
question.8.stem: The comment  i = i + 1  // add one to i  is poor because...
question.8.option.0: It repeats the code and will go stale if the line changes
question.8.option.1: Comments must be written in English
question.8.option.2: The computer runs the comment too
question.8.option.3: It should sit below the line, not beside it
question.8.why: A comment that repeats the code adds nothing and rots when the code changes; a better name removes the need for it.
